subject: Adding code to extract overall means for two categories in hierarchical model?

messages.author: 88e53569c9c42aff
messages.subject: Adding code to extract overall means for two categories in hierarchical model?
parts:
Hello,

I have only tentative/partial understanding of how to structure jags model code (the AHM book Vol. 1 has been a great help recently, thank you).  I am modeling 36 tree species distributions (presence-absence) across two time periods with covariates that are drawn from a common distribution.  Time is included in the model as a categorical covariate.  Site locations are not the same across the two time periods but are independent samples within/across the same study area.

My model code below works well to assess differences in each species' distribution across the two time periods.  However, I would like to assess whether there is an overall/aggregate difference in distributions between the two time periods, across all species (I hope this makes sense; would be glad to try to clarify what I am asking if needed).  I need help understanding how to add code to the model for this purpose.  

I have tried several approaches that generate syntax errors or compilation errors such as "Attempt to redefine node p[1]".  (I have also tried completely restructuring my code, along with my input data, based on examples in the AHM book, but have not yet figured out how to do this for my particular model needs.)

Below is the model code I have used to date (before reading the AHM book; not elegant, but does work; uses R2jags).  Covariates are time (categorical; the model is intended to compare species distributions across two time periods), elevation, elevation squared, a topographic index (lfi), and several interactions between these covariates.  There are no replicate observations at individual sites, so there is no observation model in that sense.  The model lets jags determine initial values.  Any help you can provide would be much appreciated!

mod.sp<- function () {
  for (i in 1:N) {
    presence[i] ~ dbern(p[i])
    logit(p[i]) <- B.sp[sp[i]]*int[i] + B.sp.time[sp[i]]*time[i] + B.sp.elev[sp[i]]*elev[i] + B.sp.elev2[sp[i]]*elevsq[i] + B.sp.lfi[sp[i]]*lfi[i] + B.sp.elev.lfi[sp[i]]*elev[i]*lfi[i] + B.sp.lfi.time[sp[i]]*lfi[i]*time[i] + B.sp.elev.time[sp[i]]*elev[i]*time[i] + B.sp.elev2.time[sp[i]]*elevsq[i]*time[i] + B.sp.elev2.lfi[sp[i]]*elevsq[i]*lfi[i]
  }
  for (j in 1:S) {
    B.sp[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau.sp)
    B.sp.time[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau.sp.time)
    B.sp.elev[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau.sp.elev)
    B.sp.elev2[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau.sp.elev2)
    B.sp.lfi[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau.sp.lfi)
    B.sp.elev.lfi[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau.sp.elev.lfi)
    B.sp.lfi.time[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau.sp.lfi.time)
    B.sp.elev.time[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau.sp.elev.time)
    B.sp.elev2.time[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau.sp.elev2.time)
    B.sp.elev2.lfi[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau.sp.elev2.lfi)
  }
 
  tau.sp<-pow(sigma.sp, -2)
  sigma.sp~dunif(0,10000)
  tau.sp.time<-pow(sigma.sp.time, -2)
  sigma.sp.time~dunif(0,10000)
  tau.sp.elev<-pow(sigma.sp.elev, -2)
  sigma.sp.elev~dunif(0,10000)
  tau.sp.elev2<-pow(sigma.sp.elev2, -2)
  sigma.sp.elev2~dunif(0,10000)
  tau.sp.lfi<-pow(sigma.sp.lfi, -2)
  sigma.sp.lfi~dunif(0,10000)
  tau.sp.elev.lfi<-pow(sigma.sp.elev.lfi, -2)
  sigma.sp.elev.lfi~dunif(0,10000)
  tau.sp.lfi.time<-pow(sigma.sp.lfi.time, -2)
  sigma.sp.lfi.time~dunif(0,10000)
  tau.sp.elev.time<-pow(sigma.sp.elev.time, -2)
  sigma.sp.elev.time~dunif(0,10000)
  tau.sp.elev2.time<-pow(sigma.sp.elev2.time, -2)
  sigma.sp.elev2.time~dunif(0,10000)
  tau.sp.elev2.lfi<-pow(sigma.sp.elev2.lfi, -2)
  sigma.sp.elev2.lfi~dunif(0,10000)
}

data.sp<-list(presence=presence, elev=elev, elevsq=elevsq, lfi=lfi, time=time, int=int, N=N, sp=sp, S=S)

par.sp<-c('B.sp', 'B.sp.time', 'B.sp.elev', 'B.sp.elev2', 'B.sp.lfi', 'B.sp.elev.lfi', 'B.sp.lfi.time', 'B.sp.elev.time', 'B.sp.elev2.time', 'B.sp.elev2.lfi', 'sigma.sp', 'sigma.sp.time', 'sigma.sp.elev', 'sigma.sp.elev2', 'sigma.sp.lfi', 'sigma.sp.elev.lfi', 'sigma.sp.elev.time', 'sigma.sp.elev2.time', 'sigma.sp.lfi.time', 'sigma.sp.elev2.lfi')

out.sp.fullmod <- jags(data=data.sp, parameters.to.save=par.sp, n.chains=3, n.iter=30000, n.burnin=1000, model.file=mod.sp)

messages.author: d647e6438dc3aad6
messages.subject: Re: Adding code to extract overall means for two categories in hierarchical model?
parts:
This might be overly simplistic and someone else on the list might have a better answer. However, one approach that comes to mind to assess "the overall difference in distributions between time periods across all species" would be to evaluate a non-species-specific version of B.sp.time. Let's call the new global variable B.time; it will not be indexed by species. You might create a model that includes the term B.time * time. You could keep the other variables indexed by species if you wish, but I don't think you could include both B.sp.time and B.time in the same model. However, in this case, the estimate of B.time would be affected by the sample sizes. If you have much more data for some species than others, the value of B.time would be strongly influenced by those species. (I'm not sure why time is given as time[i] in your model - is the i index for species? Does the time period of interest differ among species? If so, this might not be the right approach.)

Another option might be to keep your model as written, and then take the mean of B.sp.time. You could assign that to a new variable, like "B.mean.time <- mean(B.sp.time)" (somewhere in your model code, outside of the "for i in 1:N" loop), and then add B.mean.time to your par.sp list to record the estimate in the model output. You could likewise record sd(B.sp.time) or anything else of interest. This wouldn't have the biases resulting from uneven sample sizes, but maybe this wouldn't fully capture the nuances of the overall change between time periods.

Like I said, either option might be too simple to capture what you want to measure, but just a couple of thoughts.

Cheers,

Emily
